question: A 4-year-old boy presents with difficulty climbing stairs, toe-walking, and an unusual way of getting up from the floor (using his hands to push himself up along his legs). His maternal uncle had a similar condition and died in his early 20s. Serum creatine kinase (CK) is ordered. Which result is MOST consistent with Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

answers.text: CK 120 U/L (upper limit of normal ~200 U/L) — normal range

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A normal or mildly elevated CK makes DMD very unlikely. In DMD, CK is massively elevated due to ongoing muscle membrane disruption and fibre necrosis. A normal CK essentially excludes active DMD.

answers.text: CK 2,400 U/L (10–12 times the upper limit of normal)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While a 10-fold elevation is significant, it is on the lower end for DMD. DMD typically shows CK elevations of 10 to 100 times the upper limit of normal (commonly 10,000–20,000 U/L or higher in young, pre-symptomatic boys). A 10-fold rise is more consistent with Becker MD or another myopathy.

answers.text: CK 25,000 U/L (approximately 100 times the upper limit of normal)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In DMD, serum CK is massively elevated — typically 10 to 100 times the upper limit of normal (often 10,000–100,000 U/L). This is caused by dystrophin deficiency, which disrupts the sarcolemmal membrane, causing CK to leak from muscle cells. A CK of 25,000 U/L is characteristic of DMD in a young child with the described clinical features and X-linked family history.

answers.text: CK 400 U/L (2 times the upper limit of normal) — mildly elevated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A mild 2-fold elevation is non-specific and could be caused by vigorous exercise, intramuscular injection, or many causes of muscle injury. DMD causes a dramatically higher CK elevation (10–100× normal), making a 2-fold rise inconsistent with the diagnosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: DMD produces a CK elevation of 10–100 times the upper limit of normal. This massive elevation reflects continuous muscle membrane disruption due to dystrophin deficiency. CK is elevated even before clinical symptoms appear, making it a useful screening test in boys with motor delay or a family history of X-linked muscular dystrophy.

Correct. DMD is characterised by a massively elevated CK — typically 10 to 100 times normal (often 10,000–50,000 U/L or more). The combination of Gower's sign (using hands to climb up the legs to rise from the floor), toe-walking, proximal muscle weakness, and massive CK elevation in a young boy with X-linked family history is the diagnostic constellation of DMD.
